counterfactual_scenarios.title: What if Finn Allen had been average?
counterfactual_scenarios.change: Allen's hot streak (SR 212.8) replaced with an average opener's SR (~140) over 47 balls.
counterfactual_scenarios.original_outcome: KKR won by 8 wickets in 14.2 overs
counterfactual_scenarios.lola_outcome: KKR would still chase 143, but the chase stretches to ~17–18 overs, asking rate climbs near 9, and DC's death bowlers (Mukesh, Kuldeep) get more skin in the game. KKR likely still wins, but not at this canter.
counterfactual_scenarios.narrative: Allen scored 100 off 47 — a strike rate of 212.8 that doubled the par rate of any 14.2-over chase. Strip his SR back to a perfectly respectable 140 (a strong T20 opener) and he scores roughly 66 off the same 47 balls — about 34 runs lighter. KKR's score at the 14.2-over mark falls from 147 to ~113. They still chase 143, but they need ~30 more in the last 5.4 overs at a different complexion. Suddenly DC's death overs become consequential. Mukesh and Kuldeep — who didn't bowl a meaningful ball in this match — get the kind of pressure overs that swing IPL games. KKR likely still get there, but the comfortable 8-wicket cruise becomes a 4-or-5-wicket squeak.

counterfactual_scenarios.title: What if DC had reached 170?
counterfactual_scenarios.change: Pathum Nissanka not stumped on the wide at 10.2 — bats through to over 13 at his current SR (172). DC adds ~17 runs and finishes nearer 160.
counterfactual_scenarios.original_outcome: DC posted 142/8 — a sub-par score on a true Delhi wicket
counterfactual_scenarios.lola_outcome: DC posts ~160. KKR still chase, Allen still launches, but the 14-over winning lap becomes a 17-over fight where one wicket changes everything.
counterfactual_scenarios.narrative: Nissanka was the only DC batter who looked completely at ease — 50 off 29, with three sixes and a strike rate of 172. His dismissal was a stumping off a Anukul Roy wide at 10.2 — the kind of soft mode-of-dismissal that hurts twice. If Nissanka simply continues at his rate for one more 10-ball window, DC pick up an extra ~17 runs without changing anything else they did. Move that 142 to 160 and the chase looks different. Allen still launches — he was always going to launch — but every fielding error costs more, every dot ball matters, and KKR's middle-order players get the kind of late-chase pressure overs they rarely see. DC's batting was 30 short. Nissanka being there at 12 fixes a meaningful chunk of that gap.

game_changers.name: Finn Allen
game_changers.reason: A 47-ball century with ten sixes is a once-in-a-season innings. Allen single-handedly turned a 143-target into a 14.2-over warm-up. He didn't survive — he detonated. Every DC bowler in turn, every length, every angle.

game_changers.name: Anukul Roy
game_changers.key_stat: 4-0-31-2 — 9 dots, two key wickets in the 11th over
game_changers.reason: The 11th over was the inflexion point of DC's innings — Roy got Nissanka stumped (off a wide) and Stubbs bowled, taking two in three balls. DC went from 80/3 to 89/5 and never recovered the platform.

game_changers.name: Sunil Narine
game_changers.reason: Narine's spell was the strangulation phase. He bowled inside the powerplay and through the middle, conceded 17 across his quota, and put the asking rate that DC needed to maintain out of reach.

game_changers.name: Pathum Nissanka
game_changers.reason: The lone DC batter who looked in control. His 50 off 29 with a 172 SR was the only innings on the Delhi side that scaled the surface. Stumped off a wide at 10.2 — a soft dismissal that took the only momentum DC had.
